For an object in rotational equilibrium (not rotating, or rotating at constant angular velocity), the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that same point.
This principle is the foundation for solving problems involving balanced beams, seesaws, and levers.
For an object to be in
(neither moving nor rotating), two conditions must be satisfied:
The sum of all forces in any direction is zero (translational equilibrium).
The sum of all clockwise moments equals the sum of all anticlockwise moments about any point (rotational equilibrium).
If only the first condition is met, the object may rotate. If only the second condition is met, the object may accelerate linearly.

Two children of different masses can balance on a seesaw if the heavier child sits closer to the pivot and the lighter child sits farther away, satisfying the principle of moments.

"Moment and force are the same thing."
of a force. It depends on both the force and the distance from the pivot. A small force at a large distance can produce the same moment as a large force at a small distance.
"A larger force always produces a larger moment."
Not necessarily. If the larger force acts closer to the pivot, it may produce a smaller moment than a smaller force acting further away.
"The distance in the moment equation is the distance from the pivot to where the force is applied."
of the force. If the force is at an angle, the perpendicular distance is shorter than the direct distance.
"An object in equilibrium is not moving."
An object in equilibrium could be moving at constant velocity (translational equilibrium) or rotating at constant angular velocity (rotational equilibrium). Equilibrium means no
"Moments only matter for see-saws and beams."
Moments are relevant whenever forces cause or could cause rotation: doors, wrenches, bridges, cranes, the human body (muscles exerting forces on bones), and many engineering applications.
"The principle of moments only works when the pivot is in the middle."
The principle of moments works regardless of where the pivot is. Moments can be calculated about any point, and the principle holds for any point when the system is in equilibrium.
